Summary in one sentence: New site indexing timeline: API submission → 13 days for first crawl → 37 days for indexing → 1~4 weeks for stable search appearance. No movement in the first two weeks is normal; no indexing after a month means it’s time to investigate.

Table of Contents

  1. Complete Timeline
  2. Phase Details
  3. Factors Affecting Indexing Speed
  4. How to Check Your Current Progress
  5. When to Worry
  6. How to Accelerate Indexing
  7. Summary

Complete Timeline

From URL submission to stable search result appearance, the journey roughly goes through these phases:

Note:

  • This is the normal case timeline; new sites may take longer
  • Unlicensed GitHub Pages sites may be slower than domestically-hosted sites
  • Submission does not guarantee indexing — search engines have their own quality standards

Phase Details

Phase 1: First Crawl (Days 1~3)

After submission, the search engine adds the URL to its crawl queue. The spider waits in the queue for its turn to visit.

Things you CAN confirm at this stage:

  • ✅ Whether submission succeeded (API returns success > 0)
  • ❌ Cannot confirm if the spider has actually visited

Things that are pointless at this stage:

  • ❌ Frequently searching site:domain.com — too early, definitely no results
  • ❌ Repeatedly submitting the same URLs — wastes quota

Phase 2: Entering the Index (Days 3~7)

After the crawler fetches the page content, the search engine performs quality assessment:

Factors affecting indexing:

  • Whether the page has substantial content (not an empty page)
  • Whether content is original (not scraped/copied)
  • Page load speed
  • Mobile-friendliness

How to check: Look at the “Regular Indexing” page in the webmaster platform to see index status.

Phase 3: Stable Search Result Appearance (Weeks 1~4)

Even if a page is indexed, it doesn’t mean it will rank high in search results. New sites typically start from very low positions:

Important to understand: Search result ranking depends on content quality, external links, site authority, and many other factors. Indexing ≠ Ranking.

Factors Affecting Indexing Speed

FactorFasterSlower
Domain ageAged domains (>1 year)Newly registered domains
Hosting platformDomestic filed hostingGitHub Pages and other foreign platforms
Content qualityOriginal, valuable, frequently updatedScraped, low-quality, rarely updated
External linksLinks from authoritative sitesNo external links at all
Submission methodAPI > ManualNo submission, waiting for crawler discovery
Site structureClear sitemap + robots.txtMessy link structure

How to Check Your Current Progress

Method 1: site: Search

  • Has results → At least some pages are indexed
  • No results → Still waiting, or not indexed

Example:

Method 2: Webmaster Platform

Log into the webmaster platform to check:

  • Regular Indexing → Look at the “indexed” count
  • Crawl Diagnostics → Test whether a single URL is crawlable

Method 3: Log Analysis

If you can access server logs (GitHub Pages doesn’t provide this), you can see crawler visit records.

Reasonable Expectations by Time

TimeReasonable ExpectationUnreasonable Expectation
Day 1Submission succeededsite: shows results (impossible this fast)
Week 1Crawl may have happenedStable top-page ranking
Week 2Some pages may be indexedKeywords all have rankings
Month 1Sporadic search results start appearingHundreds of daily visitors
Month 3Steady amount of indexed contentSite is an industry authority

When to Worry

Normal (Don’t Panic)

Abnormal (Investigate)

How to Accelerate Indexing

1. Keep Producing Content

Search engines favor frequently updated sites. Publishing 1~2 articles per week is more effective than publishing 50 at once.

2. External Link Building

Publish content on these platforms with links back to your site:

  • Medium / Dev.to (for technical articles in English)
  • GitHub (add links in project READMEs)
  • Stack Overflow (reference your articles when answering questions)
  • Twitter / LinkedIn (share article links)

Search engines sometimes discover new sites through external links faster than through manual submission.

3. Good Internal Link Structure

Add “related articles” recommendations at the bottom of each article to help crawlers navigate within your site.

4. Optimize robots.txt and sitemap

Ensure the sitemap only includes pages you want indexed — exclude private pages, tag pages, etc.

Summary

PhaseTimeWhat to Do
Early (0~3 days)After submissionDon’t keep site: searching, it’s useless
Mid (1~4 weeks)Waiting for indexingKeep producing content, build external links
Late (1~3 months)StabilizationCheck indexing data, optimize content quality
Long-term (3+ months)Growth phaseBuild links, deepen content

Mindset management matters more than technical operations — SEO is a “delayed feedback” process. What you do today won’t show results for a week or even a month. Patience + consistent output = eventual indexing.

Summary: SEO isn’t magic — it’s about helping search engines better understand your site. Submitting URLs is just the first knock on the door; content quality and consistent updates are what keep you inside. Remember the timeline — no movement for a week is normal, no movement for a month means start investigating, and no movement for three months means it’s time to change strategy.

Summary in one sentence: Indexing strategy for unlicensed static sites = API submission first (use daily quota) → manual submission as backup (fill the gap) → external links to attract crawlers (long-term weight). Three phases that make the most of limited quotas.

Table of Contents

  1. Submission Method Comparison
  2. Multi-Phase Submission Strategy
  3. Quota Management Tips
  4. Key Lessons Learned
  5. FAQ

Submission Method Comparison

The webmaster platform offers three submission methods. For unlicensed GitHub Pages sites, their availability and effectiveness vary:

MethodNeeds Filing?AutomationQuotaProsCons
Sitemap submission✅ YesFully automaticUnlimitedBackground auto-crawl❌ Unavailable without filing
API submission❌ NoScript-based~10/dayProactive push, programmableSmall quota, daily limit
Manual submission❌ NoManualUnclearNo barrier, always availableOne-by-one paste, low efficiency

Why Sitemap Submission Is Unavailable

Sitemap submission requires the domain to have ICP filing. GitHub Pages .com domains cannot get filing, making this method unusable.

Note: The sitemap.xml file itself can be generated (Hexo and other tools support it), and the webmaster platform can detect it. But “submitting the sitemap” as an action requires filing.

When API Submission Fits

Best for: Moderate article counts (tens to hundreds), daily quota ~10 URLs.

Not suitable for: Large sites with tens of thousands of articles (quota too small), or users without a Python environment.

When Manual Submission Fits

Best for: Small article counts, supplementing after API quota is exhausted, or submitting single new articles on demand.

Multi-Phase Submission Strategy

Divide the site lifecycle into three phases, each with a different submission strategy:

Phase 1: New Site Initialization (Days 1~3)

Site just launched, sitemap has dozens of existing articles.

Phase 2: Routine Maintenance (Days 4~30)

After initial submissions, API quota may be exhausted (especially for unlicensed sites where quota may be a total limit).

Phase 3: Long-Tail Operations (1 month+)

Site has some content foundation; search engine crawlers may have already discovered it.

Time Investment by Phase

PhaseOperationWeekly Time
Phase 1Run API script daily1 minute
Phase 2Manual submission once a week5 minutes
Phase 3Keep producing content + external linksDepends on writing frequency

Quota Management Tips

Small Batches

With API submission, a single batch cannot exceed the remaining daily quota. For example:

Recommended batch size: 5. Check the remain field after each submission.

Prioritize Core Content

When quota is limited, prioritize these pages:

Don’t Waste Quota

Key Lessons Learned

Lesson 1: API Submission Is Not a One-Time Fix

The most common misconception: “I submitted all URLs from my sitemap today, so they’ll all be indexed tomorrow.”

The answer is: No. The daily quota (~10 URLs) means you need to run the script for multiple consecutive days to submit all pages.

Lesson 2: The Quota May Be One-Time

For unlicensed GitHub Pages sites, the API quota may be a “one-time total limit” rather than a “daily reset.”

If you find the quota doesn’t reset the next day, don’t be surprised — this isn’t a bug, it’s a limitation for unlicensed sites.

Response: Switch to manual submission and external link building once quota is exhausted.

Lesson 3: skip_render Must Be Configured for Site Verification

This is an easily overlooked but impactful detail. See the “GitHub Pages SEO Guide” article for details.

Lesson 4: Domestic Search Engines Aren’t Friendly to Foreign Hosting Platforms

PlatformSearch Engine FriendlinessNotes
GitHub Pages⭐⭐No filing, limited features
Domestic hosting⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐Can file, full features enabled
Vercel/Netlify⭐⭐Same filing limitations

If search indexing is important to you, domestic hosting + a filed domain is the optimal choice. GitHub Pages is a trade-off between “free + developer-friendly” and “SEO limitations.”

FAQ

Q: I generated sitemap.xml and the webmaster platform can detect it — can’t I just use it?

A: Detection and submission are two different things. The platform can find your sitemap via robots.txt, but the “submit” action requires ICP filing.

Q: API submission returns “over quota” — what should I do?

A: First, check if your batch size exceeds the remaining quota — ensure per-batch ≤ remaining quota. If remaining quota is already 0, you can’t submit more that day.

Q: Is there a limit on manual submission?

A: The manual submission page on the webmaster platform typically doesn’t show a clear quota, making it a good fallback when API quota runs out.

Q: How long after submitting will I see results in search?

A: New sites typically take 1~4 weeks. Submission just tells the search engine “this URL exists” — crawling, indexing, and ranking all take time.

Summary: Indexing optimization for unlicensed static sites is a “long game,” not a one-time action. Prioritize core content with the limited daily API quota, supplement with manual submission once quota is exhausted, and rely on external links and content quality to attract crawlers long-term. Mindset-wise — accept the limitations of being unlicensed and do your best within those constraints.

Summary in one sentence: GitHub Pages .com domains cannot get ICP filing, making sitemap submission and search analytics unavailable. But by combining file verification with API submission, you can still get indexed. The key is choosing the right verification method and submission channel.

Table of Contents

  1. The ICP Filing Dilemma with GitHub Pages
  2. Webmaster Platform Three-Step Setup
  3. Verification Method: File vs HTML Tag
  4. Hexo skip_render Configuration
  5. Three Submission Methods Compared
  6. Quota Limitations
  7. Maintenance Workflow
  8. Summary

The ICP Filing Dilemma with GitHub Pages

GitHub Pages assigns a xxx.github.io domain. If you bind your own .com domain (e.g., example.com), you’ll run into these issues:

FeatureNeeds ICP Filing?GitHub Pages Compatible?
Domain binding✅ Required❌ .com domains can’t file
Sitemap submission✅ Required❌ Unavailable
Search analytics✅ Required❌ Unavailable
API submission❌ Not required✅ Available
Manual submission❌ Not required✅ Available
File verification❌ Not required✅ Available

The core conflict: GitHub Pages is a foreign service and cannot obtain ICP filing from China’s MIIT. Certain advanced features on some search platforms (sitemap submission, search analytics) require a filed domain.

The good news — basic indexing features (API submission + manual submission) do not require filing.

Webmaster Platform Three-Step Setup

Step 1: Add Site

On the webmaster platform, select “Add Site” and enter your domain (e.g., https://lmlx07.github.io/tools-review).

Step 2: Verify Site Ownership

Three verification methods:

  1. File verification (recommended) → Download a verification file → Place it at your site root
  2. HTML tag verification → Add a meta tag to your homepage <head>
  3. CNAME verification → Add a TXT record to your DNS settings

For GitHub Pages, file verification is recommended.

Step 3: Submit for Indexing

Once verified, you can submit URLs (see sections below).

Verification Method: File vs HTML Tag

File Verification (Recommended)

The webmaster platform generates a verification file, e.g., baidu_verify_codeva-xxx.html.

Steps:

  1. Download the verification file
  2. Place it in your Hexo source/ directory
  3. Configure skip_render (critical!)
  4. Run hexo g -d to deploy

HTML Tag Verification

While usable, it’s trickier with Hexo — you need to modify theme templates, and theme updates can overwrite your changes.

Why File Verification Wins

AspectFile VerificationHTML Tag Verification
ComplexitySimple (drop a file)Need to modify template
PersistencePermanent (don’t delete the file)Theme updates may lose it
Impact scopeSingle fileAffects full-site template
Hexo interference⚠️ Needs skip_renderNo impact

Hexo skip_render Configuration

This is the most commonly overlooked step.

Without skip_render, Hexo’s rendering engine treats the verification file as a regular page — adding layout, header/footer HTML structure. But the search engine expects the verification file to be plain/raw HTML. Hexo’s rendered version will cause verification to fail.

Original verification file content (~32 bytes):

After Hexo rendering (~26KB):

The search engine only recognizes the first version.

Configuration

In _config.yml:

Using the wildcard * means you won’t need to change config if you switch verification files later.

Three Submission Methods Compared

MethodNeeds Filing?AutomationQuotaRecommendation
Sitemap submission✅ YesFully automatic⭐ Unlimited❌ Unavailable
API submission❌ NoScript-based~10/day⭐⭐⭐ Best choice
Manual submission❌ NoManual pasteUnclear⭐⭐ Backup

API Submission (Recommended)

Send POST requests from your local machine to the webmaster platform’s API endpoint — no server-side support needed.

How it works:

See the dedicated article “API Submission Script Development Practice” for details.

Manual Submission (Backup)

When API quota runs out, paste URLs manually on the webmaster platform’s “Manual Submission” page.

Quota Limitations

For unlicensed GitHub Pages sites, API submission has these limits:

LimitDescription
Daily quota ~10API submission allows roughly 10 URLs per day
Per-batch ≤ remaining quotaSubmitting 10 when only 7 remain will reject the entire batch
Quota may be one-timeUnlicensed GitHub Pages sites may only get a total quota, not daily reset
No sitemap submissionUnavailable due to filing requirements

Suggestion: Switch to manual submission once the API quota is exhausted.

Maintenance Workflow

After Publishing New Articles

Check Indexing Status

Tips for Faster Indexing

  1. Keep publishing: More articles and frequent updates increase your site’s search engine weight
  2. External links: Share your articles on platforms like Zhihu, Dev.to, Medium with links back to your site
  3. Manual supplementation: After API quota runs out, add manual submissions
  4. Patience: New sites typically take 1~4 weeks to get indexed

Summary

StepKey Point
Verification methodChoose file verification, place in source/ directory
Critical configMust configure skip_render or the verification file gets corrupted by Hexo
Submission methodAPI submission as primary, manual submission as backup
Expectation managementNew sites take 1~4 weeks for indexing; unlicensed sites face more restrictions

Summary: Unlicensed GitHub Pages sites can’t use sitemap submission or search analytics, but the “file verification + API submission” combination is fully capable of getting you basic indexing. The key is setting up skip_render correctly, choosing the right submission method, and maintaining reasonable expectations about indexing time.

Summary in one sentence: Idempotent automation means the script is “re-entrant” — no matter where it crashes or how many times you retry, the final state is the same. Implementation: scan completed work before starting → process only unfinished items → persist progress after each item.

The Problem

You need to batch-upload 100 chapters to a novel platform. Each chapter’s workflow:

The whole process takes 30~60 minutes. Crashes happen.

If the script crashes at chapter 57, re-running should:

  • Not duplicate: Chapters 1~56 already published → skip them
  • Not skip: Chapter 57 was interrupted → resume or skip if already done
  • Self-heal: Recover from last known state if records are lost

Core Concept

Idempotency means: no matter how many times the script crashes and restarts, the end result is the same.

Three-step strategy:

Approach 1: Local State Tracking

Persistent Record File

Filter Pending Items

Approach 2: Page State Verification

The record file can be lost. A more reliable approach: verify against the page’s current state.

Combined Approach

Complete Flow

Idempotent vs Non-Idempotent Operations

OperationIdempotent?Notes
Click “Next” button❌Clicking twice submits twice
Fill input field✅Same value, same result
Select radio✅Same selection, same result
Click “Confirm Publish”❌May create duplicates
Navigate to URL✅Same URL, same page
Read page data✅Read-only, naturally idempotent
Write progress file✅Overwrite, not append

Non-idempotent protection: Verify if the action was already performed before executing.

Summary

  1. Idempotent design isn’t a post-hoc patch — plan it from the start
  2. Triple safeguard: local record + page verification + exception retry
  3. Non-idempotent operations need guards: check state before executing
  4. Connection errors deserve special handling: reconnect and retry the current item
  5. Persist immediately: write after each item, not in batch at the end

Summary: Idempotent design upgrades automation scripts from “fragile one-shot tools” to “robust long-running services.” The concept is simple — check “what’s already done” before starting, rather than assuming “nothing is done.” Combined with persistent records and page state verification, even with network issues, browser crashes, or security software interruptions, the script runs reliably to the end.

Summary in one sentence: CDP WebSocket connections can drop due to security software, page navigation, or browser resource pressure. The solution: a “heartbeat before each operation → auto-reconnect on disconnect → retry current operation” defensive pattern.

The Problem

During long-running automation, the console suddenly shows:

The script crashes and all progress is lost. This is especially common in batch operations (e.g., uploading 100 chapters over 30+ minutes).

Root Cause Analysis

1. Security Software Interception (Most Likely)

360, Tencent PC Manager, and similar security tools may flag local WebSocket connections as threats.

Symptoms: Random disconnects with no fixed pattern.

2. Page Navigation

When CDP sends Page.navigate, Chrome briefly disconnects the old WebSocket and reconnects.

Symptoms: Disconnects always happen after Page.navigate calls.

3. Browser Resource Pressure

Chrome may reclaim resources after running for long periods with high memory usage.

4. Windows Power Management

The browser process gets suspended or its priority is lowered.

Summary in one sentence: Multi-layer dialogs (content detection → publish settings → confirmation) must be closed sequentially — an upper-layer overlay blocks interaction with lower layers. Use polling instead of fixed waits, detect visibility with offsetParent, and confirm each layer is gone before proceeding to the next.

The Problem

When publishing content on a platform, clicking “Next” triggers a cascade of dialogs:

  1. Typo warning: Detects possible typos, asks to confirm or edit
  2. Content check: Runs compliance check, offers “Basic” or “Full” scan
  3. Publish settings: Contains radio buttons (AI declaration) and a “Confirm Publish” button

These are not browser native dialogs — they’re page-level custom modals implemented with CSS overlays.

Worse: the content check takes 5~30 seconds, making fixed time.sleep() impractical.

Why Direct Clicks Fail

Issue 1: Detection Time is Unpredictable

Issue 2: Overlays Block Interaction

When the detection dialog overlay covers the page, the “Confirm Publish” button exists in the DOM but can’t be clicked:

Issue 3: Sequential Order is Mandatory

The Correct Strategy: Sequential Close + Polling

Core Pattern

Dialog Detection

Key technique: el.offsetParent !== null filters out invisible elements (closed but not DOM-removed).

Complete Handler

Complete Flow

Verification

Don’t just rely on wait_gone() — sometimes the DOM stays but the overlay is hidden:

Notes

  1. Browser native vs custom dialogs: Native alerts use Page.javascriptDialogOpening; custom overlays use the offsetParent polling method above

Summary in one sentence: React controlled components hijack the input’s value property — el.value = x won’t update React state. The fix: obtain the native value setter via Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype, 'value').set, set the value bypassing React, then dispatch input/change events to trigger React’s state sync.

The Problem

On a novel platform’s author dashboard, I needed to auto-fill chapter titles. The most intuitive approach:

The input field displayed the text visually, but when clicking “Save,” React received an empty value. The DOM showed the value, but React’s internal state didn’t reflect it.

How React Controlled Components Work

React controlled components work like this:

React overrides the value property’s getter and setter on each input instance:

  1. Direct el.value = x → calls React’s overridden setter → React ignores it
  2. User input → triggers input event → React captures event → calls setState → updates value

The key insight: React listens for events, not property changes. Simply changing the property doesn’t fire events, so React doesn’t know the value changed.

Failed Attempts

Why does dispatching an input event still fail? Because React overrides the value getter — el.value returns React’s state value, not the actual DOM property. When the event fires, React reads the getter and gets the old value.

The Correct Approach: Native Setter Bypass

The solution: get the native value setter that existed before React overrode it, use it to set the value, then dispatch events to trigger React sync.

Step-by-step Explanation

  1. Object.getOwnPropertyDescriptor(HTMLInputElement.prototype, 'value').set

    • Gets the setter from the prototype level (before React overrides it per-instance)
    • React overrides the setter on each element instance, not on the prototype

  2. nativeSetter.call(el, value)

    • Applies the native setter to the specific element
    • Bypasses React’s instance-level getter/setter, directly modifying the real DOM property

  3. el.dispatchEvent(new Event('input', {bubbles: true}))

    • React listens for input events to sync state
    • After the event fires, React’s onChange handler runs setState with the correct value

Complete Example

Complete Wrapper Class

Similar Issues in Other Frameworks

FrameworkIssueSolution
ReactOverrides value getter/setterNative setter + input event
Vuev-model bindingSame approach
AngularngModel bindingSame approach
Arco DesignCustom input componentMay need additional custom events

Summary

  1. React controlled components ignore el.value = x because React overrides the value property
  2. The fix: obtain the native setter from HTMLInputElement.prototype, bypass React’s interception
  3. Must dispatch events: fire input + change after setting to trigger React state sync
  4. Textarea works the same way using HTMLTextAreaElement.prototype.value
  5. Focus first: some libraries require the input to be focused before accepting input

Summary: Understanding React’s controlled component mechanism — where value getters/setters are overridden — is the key to solving this. The native setter bypass + event notification pattern works not only for React but also for Vue, Angular, and other frameworks using similar mechanisms.

问题场景

为什么 JS click 不行

Radix UI 使用 portal 将下拉菜单内容渲染到 document.body 下（而非在按钮的DOM树中）。它的交互机制依赖真实 pointer 事件链：

  • pointerdown → pointerup → mousedown → mouseup → click

而 element.click() 是合成事件，只会触发 click，不会触发前面的一串 pointer 事件。Radix UI 的内部状态机监听的是 pointer 事件，合成事件无法触发它的状态变更。

element.click()❌❌
CDP dispatchMouseEvent✅✅
真实用户点击✅✅

这就是问题的根源。

步骤 1：CDP 鼠标点击打开菜单

步骤 2：JS click 选择菜单项

有意思的是——菜单项虽然通过 portal 渲染，但它在 DOM 中已经存在且正常渲染，JS click 对它有效：

步骤 3：Escape 关闭菜单

关键发现：Radix UI 下拉菜单选择选项后不会自动关闭。菜单仍然显示在页面上，会遮挡后续操作。必须手动发送 Escape 关闭：

完整封装

教训总结

  1. 不要只用 JS click：现代 UI 组件库（Radix UI、React Aria、MUI）依赖真实 pointer 事件，合成事件不触发状态变更
  2. CDP 鼠标点击 + JS click 混合使用：打开菜单用 CDP 鼠标，选择选项用 JS click——各取所长
  3. Escape 关闭是必要步骤：portal 菜单不会自动消失，不关闭会遮挡后续操作

Summary in one sentence: CDP is the “assembly language” of browser automation — the most powerful and the most verbose. Playwright is the “high-level programming language” — easy to use but sacrifices some control. Choose based on how much control you need and how much complexity you can tolerate.

Architecture Differences

Raw CDP Approach

CDP (Chrome DevTools Protocol) is the native debugging protocol exposed by Chrome. The raw approach means your code communicates directly with the browser via WebSocket with zero abstraction layers.

This is the CDP helper function used throughout this article series:

The core flow:

  1. Fetch the target page’s WebSocket URL from http://localhost:9222/json
  2. Establish a WebSocket connection using the websockets library
  3. Manually construct JSON commands and send them via ws.send()
  4. Match responses by id field to retrieve results

Key characteristic: You handle everything yourself — connection management, command framing, response matching, error handling, lifecycle management.

Playwright Approach

Playwright also uses CDP under the hood (for Chromium), but adds three layers of abstraction:

Playwright handles a massive amount of low-level details for developers:

  • Auto-waiting: All actions automatically wait for elements to be ready — no manual sleep() calls needed
  • State management: Automatically manages browser instance, context, and page lifecycles
  • Cross-browser compatibility: Same API works across Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit
  • Smart retry: Failed operations auto-retry with built-in timeout mechanisms
  • Event system: Browser events exposed as native Python callbacks

Code Comparison: Same Tasks, Different Approaches

Below we compare the code volume and complexity of both approaches across three typical tasks.

Task 1: Navigation and Screenshot

Raw CDP:

Playwright:

Raw CDP is ~40 lines, Playwright is 12 lines. Playwright wraps environment setup, connection management, and protocol interaction into clean API calls.

Task 2: Network Interception

Intercept image requests and count them.

Raw CDP:

Playwright:

With raw CDP, you must manually manage event listeners. WebSocket messages mix command responses and events in a single stream, requiring careful filtering. Playwright provides a clean page.on() event API.

Task 3: Intercept and Modify Responses

Replace all images on a page with a placeholder.

Raw CDP:

Playwright:

Playwright’s page.route() API turns the common need of “intercept matching requests and modify responses” into a single function call. Raw CDP requires manual handling of interception IDs, constructing raw HTTP responses, and managing the async event loop.

When to Choose CDP

1. Maximum Control

Raw CDP exposes every corner of the Chrome debugging protocol. Some low-level features Playwright does not expose directly:

2. Anti-Detection Requirements

For security testing and anti-crawling scenarios, raw CDP is harder to detect than Playwright. Playwright leaves automation traces in the browser context — navigator.webdriver handling differs from native CDP.

3. Custom Browser Startup Parameters

Some scenarios require non-standard CDP commands or custom launch parameters. Raw CDP has no framework limitations — you can freely combine any protocol commands.

4. Educational Value

Understanding CDP is the best way to master browser automation. When you encounter problems that Playwright cannot solve, CDP knowledge is your “escape hatch.”

When to Choose Playwright

1. Cross-Browser Support

Playwright’s biggest advantage: one codebase that runs on Chromium, Firefox, and WebKit.

Raw CDP can only control Chromium-based browsers (Chrome, Edge, Brave, etc.).

2. Auto-Waiting Mechanism

All Playwright operations have built-in auto-waiting:

3. Stable API and Toolchain

Playwright provides a complete, out-of-the-box ecosystem:

  • Auto browser download: playwright install automatically downloads browsers
  • Built-in assertions: expect(page.locator(...)).to_be_visible()
  • Test runner: Playwright Test with built-in reporting, retries, parallel execution
  • Codegen: playwright codegen records user operations to generate scripts
  • Trace Viewer: Visual debugging of test failures

4. Team Collaboration and Maintainability

If multiple developers are involved, Playwright’s declarative API is much easier to maintain and review than raw CDP.

Command Latency

Playwright’s extra overhead comes from:

  1. API layer wrapping: Python method calls to internal CDP command generation to serialization to WebSocket send
  2. Auto-waiting checks: Element state verification before each operation
  3. Event management: Playwright maintains its own event queue and state synchronization

Controlling 10 concurrent browser pages for scraping:

Summary and Decision Framework

Choosing between CDP and Playwright depends on your core requirements:

Final Recommendations

In most cases, the Playwright + CDPSession hybrid approach is the optimal path. You use Playwright for 80% of routine tasks, and when you hit Playwright’s boundaries, you drop into the protocol layer via CDPSession to solve the problem.

If your project requires maximum anti-detection capability (like browser fingerprint evasion in security testing), raw CDP is the better fit. This comes with higher development costs and maintenance complexity.

Core principle: Use Playwright to build applications, use CDP knowledge to fight fires. They are not competitors — they are complementary partners. Understanding CDP lets you truly master Playwright; using Playwright well keeps you from getting lost in CDP’s low-level details.

  1. Multi-Instance vs Multi-Tab: The Fundamental Difference

Multi-Instance vs Multi-Tab: The Fundamental Difference

Before diving in, let’s clarify an important distinction:

AspectMulti-Tab (One Process)Multi-Instance (Multiple Processes)
Processes1 Chrome processN independent Chrome processes
IsolationShared cookies, cache, rendererFully isolated
Memory costLow (shared main process)High (~100-300MB each)
Crash impactOne tab crash doesn’t affect othersOne instance crash doesn’t affect others
FingerprintAll tabs share the same fingerprintEach instance can have a unique fingerprint
CDP debug portShared (e.g., 9222)Unique port per instance
Use casesLight crawlers, simple testsLarge-scale parallel, isolation testing, anti-bot

One sentence difference: Multi-tab runs inside one browser process; multi-instance runs across separate processes.

Our previous articles covered multi-tab scenarios — managing multiple pages within a single Chrome process. This article shifts to the multi-process level, discussing how to orchestrate multiple independent Chrome processes.

Why You Need Multiple Chrome Instances

1. Complete Isolation

Browser fingerprinting tools (like fingerprintjs) can detect shared underlying properties across tabs within the same process — WebGL renderer, font list, timezone data, etc. Different Chrome instances naturally have independent rendering contexts. Combined with separate --user-data-dir directories, you also get fully isolated cookies and storage.

2. Parallel Speedup

Suppose you need to capture 100 pages or log into 50 accounts for batch operations. A single-process multi-tab approach is constrained by Chrome’s rendering thread and memory, making large-scale parallelism difficult. Multi-instance orchestration lets you fully utilize multi-core CPUs for true horizontal scaling.

3. Different Configurations / Fingerprints

Each instance can be independently configured with:

  • Different --user-data-dir (separate browser profiles)
  • Different User-Agent, viewport
  • Different proxy (--proxy-server)
  • Different language, timezone (startup flags or CDP injection)

This is critical for anti-bot crawling, ad verification, and multi-account management.

4. Test Environment Isolation

In E2E testing, when multiple test cases run in parallel, multi-instance prevents cross-test state contamination — one test’s login state won’t accidentally affect another.

Port Management: One Debug Port Per Instance

The CDP debug port is the unique identifier for each Chrome instance. Port assignment is the first step in multi-instance orchestration.

Port Selection Strategy

Guidelines:

  • Avoid common ports (80, 443, 8080) to prevent conflicts
  • Start from 9222 and increment
  • Check port availability before launching

Launching Chrome Instances and Tracking PIDs

Use subprocess.Popen to launch Chrome, assigning an independent port and user data directory to each instance.

Why Tracking PIDs Matters

Each instance’s PID is critical for management:

  • Sending termination signals
  • Detecting zombie processes

Summary

Through this article, you have mastered the core skills of CDP multi-instance orchestration:

  • Multi-instance vs multi-tab: Understanding process-level isolation and when to use each
  • Port and process management: Assigning unique ports and tracking PIDs
  • Launch and discovery: subprocess launch + HTTP-based WebSocket URL discovery
  • Connection pooling: asyncio WebSocket connection management
  • Task distribution strategies: Round-robin, least-loaded, weighted

Core principle: Multi-instance is a “heavy weapon” — higher memory overhead and slower startup — but the isolation and parallelism it provides are impossible to achieve with multi-tab alone. Choose the right granularity for your scenario: use multi-tab for lightweight daily tasks; deploy multi-instance when you need isolation, high-performance parallelism, or anti-detection capabilities.

From Interception to Filtering: The Mindset Shift

If you have read our previous article CDP Network Interception and Request Tampering, you already know the basics of capturing and modifying requests with CDP. But intercepting and filtering are two different things:

  • Interception: I can catch a request, and I can optionally modify or release it
  • Filtering: I have a rule system that automatically decides the fate of every request

A content filter is essentially a rule engine + async decision system. It receives each request’s URL, resource type, domain, and other information, then produces a decision through rule matching:

Real-world content filters (uBlock Origin, AdBlock Plus) all follow this pattern. With CDP, we can implement a fully programmable version in code.

Why the Fetch Domain Is the Best Foundation

Mode Selection Guide
